payload.rationale: The YES event requires October 2026 seasonally adjusted U-3 to be reported above 4.3%—normally 4.4% or higher at the published one-decimal precision. A reported 4.3% does not qualify. No current labor-market observations are supplied, so this is a weak prior-based judgment, not a forecast anchored to the latest unemployment release. General background about low-4% unemployment in the mid-2020s puts this threshold within a plausible range. I assume substantial labor-market persistence, while allowing modestly more weight to labor-market weakening than renewed tightening, yielding a probability slightly above one-half. The strongest reason this estimate could be too high is that unemployment may currently be comfortably below the threshold, with resilient hiring keeping October at 4.3% or less. The strongest reason it could be too low is that unemployment may already be above the threshold or rising amid weakening hiring; persistence would then make YES substantially more likely.
limitations: No current research or observations were supplied, including the latest U-3 rate, payroll growth, or unemployment claims.
The assumed level and direction of labor-market conditions are uncertain; missing current data dominate the forecast uncertainty.
Household-survey sampling variability and published rounding can determine which side of this narrow threshold the reported rate falls on.
Detailed frozen rules were not supplied beyond the event definition; this estimate targets the specified BLS October 2026 report rather than a later revised value.
